newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Reliance unveils bonus, sees bright future.
newsitem.headline: India's Reliance unveils bonus, sees bright future.

text.p: Petrochemicals and textile giant Reliance Industries on Thursday doled out a handsome reward to its shareholders and predicted sales would more than double by the turn of the century.
Reliance, an aggressive borrower in global capital markets, also announced it would adopt international accounting standards.
Chairman Dhirubhai Ambani ended weeks of feverish stock market guessing when he announced a one-for-one bonus share issue at a packed annual shareholders meeting.

"I would like to announce my dear shareholders I am delighted to report to you that after due deliberation and considering your suggestions, the board has recommended a bonus issue in the ratio of 1:1," Ambani told cheering shareholders.
Reliance is India's largest private-sector corporation and boasts 2.6 million shareholders.
"Let the rivers of bonus and dividends flow," shareholder Ashalata Maheshwari told the meeting just before Ambani called an adjournment so the board could discuss the bonus issue.
It took the company's directors only a few minutes to agree the historic handout.
"A bonus offer reflects our confidence in the future earnings growth of the company," Ambani said.

Reliance shares -- which have surged some 85 percent on the Bombay bourse this calendar year -- responded by leaping to a new 52-week high of 388 rupees. Profit taking near the close erased some gains and the shares ended 11.0 rupees up at 377.50.
A confident Ambani predicted sales would touch nearly 200 billion rupees ($5.5 billion) by 2000. Sales in the year ended March 31 totalled 87.3 billion rupees, up from 77.86 billion in 1995/96.
Reliance began life as a commodities trading firm in 1958, and under the control of the Ambani family built itself into India's largest private sector company.
"We do not foresee any further equity dilution over the next two to three years, excluding outstanding conversions (of debentures)," Ambani told shareholders.
He said he favoured a share buyback programme and would examine this option as soon as the government legislated promised changes to the Companies Act.
Ambani said the firm recognised the need to improve capital efficiency as measured by return on equity and earnings growth.
"We have set ourselves the targets of achieving a 20 percent compounded growth in earnings per share and a return of 20 percent of shareholders funds over the next five years."
Analysts said the projections were above their estimates.
"Ambani has made a lot of promises which people will like," said an analyst at a leading U.S. brokerage.

"He's projected an earnings growth of 20 percent, talked about buy back and no equity dilution -- all these are positive things," he said, adding that he expected earnings to grow at a more modest 17.5 percent.

In a recent report on Reliance, Goldman Sachs and its Indian affiliate Kotak Securities said the increased burden of finance charges due to the firm's aggressive expansion plans and falling margins in petrochemicals will hit earnings growth.
Earnings per share were likely to grow by 10.6 percent in the current 1997/98 financial year, and would fall by 6.2 percent in 1998/99, the report said.

"The company has cash flows sufficient for projects they have in mind and they can manage with debt till 1998/98," said Kotak analyst Sanjeev Prasad, reacting to Ambani's statement on no immediate equity dilutions.
Prasad said he was maintaining his earnings forecasts for the time being.
Analysts said the robust earnings projects were unlikely to translate into a giant surge in the stock's price.
"Today's bonus news will be good for sentiment but the stock has gone up quite a bit and we expect the price to stabilise in this range in the coming months," said the analyst at the U.S. brokerage.
